stem: One root of the equation \(\begin{vmatrix} 3x-8 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3x-8 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3x-8 \end{vmatrix} = 0\) is
solution: For a \(3\times 3\) determinant with diagonal entries \(d=3x-8\) and every off-diagonal entry \(e=3\), the value is \((d-e)^2(d+2e)=(3x-11)^2(3x-2)\). Setting it to \(0\) gives \(x=\dfrac{11}{3}\) or \(x=\dfrac{2}{3}\). Among the options, \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) is a root. Matches option B.

stem: The equations \(x+2y+3z=1\), \(x-y+4z=0\), \(2x+y+7z=1\) have
solution: The coefficient determinant is \(0\) because the third row equals the sum of the first two rows. The same combination holds for the constants (\(1+0=1\), the RHS of the third equation), so the third equation is dependent and the system is consistent with infinitely many solutions. Matches option D.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: If \(x,y,z\) are different and \(\begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1+x^3 \\ y & y^2 & 1+y^3 \\ z & z^2 & 1+z^3 \end{vmatrix}=0\), then \(xyz=\)
solution: Split column 3 into \(1\) and \(x^3\): the determinant becomes \(V+xyz\,V=V(1+xyz)\), where \(V=\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^2\\1&y&y^2\\1&z&z^2\end{vmatrix}\) is the Vandermonde determinant. Since \(x,y,z\) are distinct, \(V\neq 0\), so \(1+xyz=0\), giving \(xyz=-1\). Matches option C.

subtopic: Special Matrices — Skew-Symmetric, Diagonal, Idempotent, Orthogonal, Rotation
stem: If \(a_i^2+b_i^2+c_i^2=1\) for \(i=1,2,3\) and \(a_ia_j+b_ib_j+c_ic_j=0\) for \(i\neq j\), then the value of \(\begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}^2\) is
solution: The conditions say the columns of the matrix are orthonormal, so the matrix is orthogonal and its determinant is \(\pm 1\). Hence the square of the determinant is \(1\). Matches option C.

subtopic: Linear Systems — Consistency, Cramer's Rule, Solution Space
stem: If the system of linear equations \(x+2ay+az=0\), \(x+3by+bz=0\), \(x+4cy+cz=0\) has a non-zero solution, then \(a,b,c\) are in
solution: A non-zero (non-trivial) solution needs the coefficient determinant to vanish. Expanding gives \(ab+bc-2ac=0\); dividing by \(abc\) yields \(\dfrac1a+\dfrac1c=\dfrac2b\), so \(a,b,c\) are in H.P. Matches option C.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: If \(m\) is a positive integer and \(\Delta_r=\begin{vmatrix} 2r-1 & {}^{m}C_r & 1 \\ m^2-1 & 2^m & m+1 \\ \sin^2(m^2) & \sin^2(m) & \sin^2(m+1) \end{vmatrix}\), then the value of \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m}\Delta_r\) is
solution: Only the first row depends on \(r\). Summing it: \(\sum_{r=0}^{m}(2r-1)=m^2-1\), \(\sum_{r=0}^{m}{}^{m}C_r=2^m\), \(\sum_{r=0}^{m}1=m+1\). This makes the first row identical to the second row, so the determinant is \(0\). Matches option A.

subtopic: Linear Systems — Consistency, Cramer's Rule, Solution Space
stem: The system of equations \(x+2y+3z=4\), \(2x+3y+4z=5\), \(3x+4y+5z=6\) has
solution: The coefficient determinant is \(0\) (the rows are in A.P., so row 1 + row 3 = 2(row 2)). The constants satisfy the same relation (\(4+6=2\cdot 5\)), so the system is consistent and dependent, giving infinitely many solutions. Matches option A.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: If \(A,B,C\) are the angles of a non-right-angled triangle \(ABC\), then \(\begin{vmatrix} \tan A & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \tan B & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \tan C \end{vmatrix}\) is equal to
solution: Expanding gives \(\tan A\tan B\tan C-(\tan A+\tan B+\tan C)+2\). In a triangle \(\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C\), so the expression equals \(2\). Matches option B.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: Let \(A=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \sin\theta & 1 \\ -\sin\theta & 1 & \sin\theta \\ -1 & -\sin\theta & 1 \end{vmatrix}\), where \(0\le\theta\le 2\pi\). Then the range of \(|A|\) is
solution: Expanding gives \(|A|=2+2\sin^2\theta\). Since \(\sin^2\theta\in[0,1]\), the range is the closed interval \([2,4]\). NOTE: the printed options (a), (b), (c) are all identical \((2,4)\) in the source paper, so the question is defective; the correct range is \([2,4]\) and option D is keyed by default.
reviewNote: FLAWED in source: options a/b/c are printed identically as (2,4). True range is the closed interval [2,4]. Excluded from the practice bank; key D is a best-guess for OMR parity — verify against the LWS key.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: If \(a,b,c\) are unequal, the condition that the value of the determinant \(\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} a & a^2 & a^3+1 \\ b & b^2 & b^3+1 \\ c & c^2 & c^3+1 \end{vmatrix}=0\) is
solution: Splitting column 3 gives \(\Delta=V+abc\,V=V(1+abc)\), where \(V\) is the Vandermonde determinant. Since \(a,b,c\) are unequal, \(V\neq 0\), so \(1+abc=0\), i.e. \(abc=-1\). Matches option C.

subtopic: Linear Systems — Consistency, Cramer's Rule, Solution Space
stem: If the system \(2x+5y+8z=0\), \(x+4y+7z=0\), \(6x+4y-\lambda z=0\) has a non-trivial solution, then \(\lambda\) is equal to
solution: A non-trivial solution needs the coefficient determinant to be \(0\): \(\begin{vmatrix}2&5&8\\1&4&7\\6&4&-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=-3\lambda-6=0\), so \(\lambda=-2\). Matches option B.

stem: The value of a third-order determinant is 11. Then the value of the square of the determinant formed by its cofactors is
solution: For an \(n\)-th order determinant, the determinant of the cofactor matrix is \((\det A)^{n-1}\). For \(n=3\) this is \(11^2=121\). Its square is \(121^2=14641\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), then \(\det(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A))\) is
solution: For an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(\det(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A))=|A|^{(n-1)^2}\). Here \(|A|=14\) and \(n=3\), so the value is \(14^{4}\). Matches option A.

stem: If \(A\) is a non-singular matrix, then \(\det(A^{-1})=\)
solution: \(\det(A^{-1})=\dfrac{1}{\det(A)}\). Matches option D.
From \(A^2+A-I=0\) we get \(A(A+I)=I\), so \(A^{-1}=A+I=I+A\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(A\) is a \(3\times 3\) matrix and \(\det(3A)=k\,\det(A)\), then \(k=\)
solution: \(\det(3A)=3^3\det(A)=27\det(A)\), so \(k=27\). Matches option D.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: If \(\alpha,\beta\) are non-real numbers satisfying \(x^3-1=0\), then the value of \(\begin{vmatrix} \lambda+1 & \alpha & \beta \\ \alpha & \lambda+\beta & 1 \\ \beta & 1 & \lambda+\alpha \end{vmatrix}\) is equal to
solution: \(\alpha,\beta\) are the non-real cube roots of unity, so \(\alpha+\beta=-1\), \(\alpha\beta=1\), \(\alpha^3=\beta^3=1\), and \(\alpha^2+\beta^2=-1\). Expanding the determinant and simplifying with these relations gives \(\lambda^3\). Matches option B.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
stem: \(\begin{vmatrix} x+1 & x+2 & x+\lambda \\ x+2 & x+3 & x+\mu \\ x+3 & x+4 & x+\nu \end{vmatrix}=0\), where \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\) are in A.P., is
optA: An equation whose all roots are real
optC: An equation with only one real root
solution: Since \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\) are in A.P., \(\lambda-2\mu+\nu=0\). The row operations \(R_1-R_2\) and \(R_2-R_3\) produce two identical rows, so the determinant is \(0\) for every \(x\) — an identity in \(x\). Matches option B.

stem: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2y & z \\ x & y & -z \\ x & -y & z \end{pmatrix}\) and \(A'A=I\). Then the value of \(x^2+y^2+z^2\) is
solution: \(A'A=I\) makes the columns orthonormal: \(2x^2=1\), \(6y^2=1\), \(3z^2=1\). So \(x^2+y^2+z^2=\dfrac12+\dfrac16+\dfrac13=1\). Matches option A.

stem: The value of \(x\) for which the matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) is the inverse of \(B=\begin{pmatrix} -x & 14x & 7x \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ x & -4x & -2x \end{pmatrix}\) is
solution: \(AB=I\) requires \((AB)_{11}=2(-x)+7x=5x=1\), so \(x=\dfrac15\). The remaining entries are consistent with this. Matches option D.

stem: If \(A_r=\begin{pmatrix} r & r-1 \\ r-1 & r \end{pmatrix}\), \(r\in N\), then \(|A_1|+|A_2|+|A_3|+\cdots+|A_{2006}|\) is
solution: \(|A_r|=r^2-(r-1)^2=2r-1\). The sum of the first \(2006\) odd numbers is \(2006^2\). Matches option B.

stem: If \(A=[a_{ij}]_{3\times 3}\), \(B=[b_{ij}]_{2\times 2}\), \(C=[c_{ij}]_{3\times 3}\) are three matrices with \(|A|=3\), \(|B|=-2\), \(|C|=4\), then \(|ABC|\) is
solution: The product \(ABC\) requires \(A_{3\times 3}B_{2\times 2}\), but a \(3\times 3\) matrix cannot be multiplied by a \(2\times 2\) matrix (the inner dimensions \(3\) and \(2\) differ). So \(ABC\) is not defined. Matches option D.

stem: If \(A\) and \(B\) are two skew-symmetric matrices of order \(n\), then
optC: \(AB\) is a symmetric matrix if \(A\) and \(B\) commute
solution: \((AB)^T=B^TA^T=(-B)(-A)=BA\). So \(AB\) is symmetric iff \(AB=BA\), i.e. iff \(A\) and \(B\) commute. Matches option C.

stem: If the product of the matrix \(B=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 6 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) with a matrix \(A\) has inverse \(C=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\), then \(A^{-1}\) equals
solution: From \((BA)^{-1}=C\) we get \(A^{-1}B^{-1}=C\), so \(A^{-1}=CB=\begin{pmatrix} -3 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 14 & 6 \end{pmatrix}\). NOTE: this true value matches NO option exactly — option (d) agrees in rows 2 and 3 but prints \(-3\) instead of \(-5\) at position (1,2); option (c) has the correct first row but a wrong (2,2) entry. The printed options carry an error; option D is the closest (two of three rows correct).

stem: The matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \omega & \omega^2 \\ \omega & \omega^2 & 1 \\ \omega^2 & 1 & \omega \end{pmatrix}\), where \(\omega\) is a cube root of unity, is a
solution: The matrix equals its own transpose (entry \((i,j)\) equals entry \((j,i)\) for every pair), so it is a symmetric matrix. Matches option B.

stem: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\) be two matrices such that \(AB=BA\) and \(c\neq 0\). Then the value of \(\dfrac{a-d}{3b-c}\) is
solution: \(AB=BA\) gives \(3b=2c\) and \(c=d-a\). Then \(3b-c=2c-c=c\) and \(a-d=-c\), so \(\dfrac{a-d}{3b-c}=\dfrac{-c}{c}=-1\). Matches option D.

stem: Consider matrices \(A,B,C,D\) of orders \(2\times 3,\ 3\times 4,\ 4\times 4,\ 4\times 2\) respectively. Let \(x=(\alpha\,A\,B\,\gamma\,C^2 D)^3\), where \(\alpha,\gamma\) are scalars. If \(|x|=k\,|ABC^2D|^3\), then \(k\) is
solution: \(ABC^2D\) is a \(2\times 2\) matrix and \(x=(\alpha\gamma)^3(ABC^2D)^3\). For a \(2\times 2\) matrix, \(|sM|=s^2|M|\), so \(|x|=((\alpha\gamma)^3)^2|ABC^2D|^3=\alpha^6\gamma^6\,|ABC^2D|^3\). Hence \(k=\alpha^6\gamma^6\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(A=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), then \(\operatorname{adj}A=\)
solution: Here \(AA^T=9I\), so \(A^{-1}=\dfrac{A^T}{9}\), and \(|A|=27\). Then \(\operatorname{adj}A=|A|A^{-1}=27\cdot\dfrac{A^T}{9}=3A^T\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(A\) satisfies the equation \(x^3-5x^2+4x+k=0\), then \(A^{-1}\) exists if
solution: From \(A^3-5A^2+4A+kI=0\) we get \(A(A^2-5A+4I)=-kI\); \(A^{-1}\) exists iff \(k\neq 0\). Since none of the listed conditions is \(k\neq 0\), the answer is 'None'. Matches option D.

stem: If \(B\) is a non-singular matrix and \(A\) is a square matrix of the same size, then \(\det(B^{-1}AB)=\)
solution: \(\det(B^{-1}AB)=\det(B^{-1})\det(A)\det(B)=\det(A)=|A|\). Matches option D.

stem: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix} x & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & y & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & z \end{pmatrix}\). If \(xyz=60\) and \(8x+4y+3z=20\), then \(A(\operatorname{adj}A)\) is equal to
solution: \(A(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|I\). Expanding, \(|A|=xyz-8x-4y-3z+28=60-(8x+4y+3z)+28=60-20+28=68\). So \(A(\operatorname{adj}A)=68I\). Matches option C.

stem: If \(A\) is a non-singular matrix of order \(3\times 3\), then \(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)\) is equal to
solution: For order \(n\), \(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|^{n-2}A\). For \(n=3\) this is \(|A|A\). Matches option A.

subtopic: Linear Systems — Consistency, Cramer's Rule, Solution Space
stem: If \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -6 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\), then \((x,y,z)\) is equal to
solution: The right side evaluates to \((6,-6,0)^T\). Solving \(x+2y+3z=6\), \(3x+y+2z=-6\), \(2x+3y+z=0\) gives \(x=-4,\ y=2,\ z=2\). Matches option A.

stem: Matrix \(M_r\) is defined as \(M_r=\begin{pmatrix} r & r-1 \\ r-1 & r \end{pmatrix}\), \(r\in N\). Then \(\det(M_1)+\det(M_2)+\cdots+\det(M_{2009})=\)
solution: \(\det(M_r)=r^2-(r-1)^2=2r-1\). The sum of the first \(2009\) odd numbers is \(2009^2\). Matches option B.

stem: If \(A=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), then \(A+2A^T\) equals
solution: \(A\) is skew-symmetric, so \(A^T=-A\). Then \(A+2A^T=A-2A=-A=A^T\). Matches option A.
reviewNote: Option (b) is printed as a garbled '2^2' in the source; reconstructed as 2A. The key (A) is unaffected. Verify option (b) text against the LWS paper.

stem: The inverse of the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) is
solution: \(|A|=1\). The adjoint (transpose of the cofactor matrix) is \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 \\ -2 & -4 & -5 \end{pmatrix}\), which is the inverse since \(|A|=1\). Matches option B.

subtopic: Linear Systems — Consistency, Cramer's Rule, Solution Space
stem: If \(t\) is a real number and \(k=\dfrac{t^2-t+1}{t^2+t+1}\), then the system \(3x-y+4z=3\), \(x+2y-3z=-2\), \(6x+5y+kz=-3\), for any allowable value of \(k\), has
solution: For real \(t\), \(k\) lies in \(\left[\dfrac13,3\right]\). The coefficient determinant equals \(7(k+5)\), which is non-zero for every \(k\) in this range, so the system has a unique solution. Matches option A.

subtopic: Special Matrices — Skew-Symmetric, Diagonal, Idempotent, Orthogonal, Rotation
stem: If \(A=\begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ b & c & a \\ c & a & b \end{pmatrix}\), \(abc=1\) and \(A^TA=I\), then the value of \(a^3+b^3+c^3\) (where \(a,b,c>0\)) is
solution: \(A^TA=I\) gives \(a^2+b^2+c^2=1\) and \(ab+bc+ca=0\), so \((a+b+c)^2=1\) and \(a+b+c=1\). Using \(a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca)=1\), we get \(a^3+b^3+c^3=1+3abc=1+3=4\). Matches option D.

stem: If \(A\) and \(B\) are non-singular square matrices of the same order \(3\times 3\), then which one of the following is correct?
solution: For \(3\times 3\), \(|\operatorname{adj}M|=|M|^2\). With \(m=|AB|\): \(|\operatorname{adj}((AB)^{-1})|=|(AB)^{-1}|^2=m^{-2}\) and \(|(\operatorname{adj}(AB))^{-1}|=|\operatorname{adj}(AB)|^{-1}=m^{-2}\). These are equal, so option C is correct.
